captions: Chapter nine — commodities.
Beyond stocks lies a parallel market — real,
physical things: gold, silver, crude oil, metals.
In India these trade on the MCX.
Let's learn how,
and why gold in particular belongs in a portfolio.
So, what are commodities?
Raw, physical goods, grouped into families.
First, bullion — gold and silver.
These are safe-haven assets,
stores of wealth that people flee to in uncertain times.
Second, energy — crude oil and natural gas,
driven by OPEC decisions, demand, and geopolitics.
Third, base metals — copper, zinc, aluminium —
the industrial metals that rise and fall with global growth and,
especially, China.
In India, these trade on the MCX,
the Multi Commodity Exchange — the largest, and,
like the stock market, regulated by SEBI.
One big difference: because commodities track global markets,
the MCX stays open far longer —
from about nine in the morning until nearly midnight,
around eleven fifty-five p m,
so it can react to overnight news from around the world.
That long window, plus leverage, makes commodities a fast,
demanding market.
How do you actually trade a commodity?
Almost always through futures — you trade a contract,
not a vault of gold.
The contracts come in standardised lot sizes.
Gold, for instance, has a main one-kilogram contract,
and a smaller Gold Mini of one hundred grams so ordinary traders can take part.
As with stock futures, you pay only a small margin —
a fraction of the contract's value —
which means the same double-edged leverage.
A small favourable move is magnified; so is an unfavourable one.
And what moves commodity prices?
Global forces.
Gold and silver respond to the US dollar,
to real interest rates, and to geopolitical fear — plus,
in India, the huge festival and wedding demand.
Crude follows OPEC and the world economy.
Base metals follow global growth.
This is a macro trader's arena —
you're really trading world events.
Here is the most useful commodity idea for a normal investor: you do not have to touch the leverage at all.
You can own gold simply, without a futures contract.
A gold ETF holds gold in your demat account — no storage,
no leverage, sell it in one click.
A Sovereign Gold Bond is government-issued gold that even pays you a small interest on top.
Both are calm, non-leveraged ways to own gold.
Why own gold at all?
Because of its role as a hedge.
Gold often rises exactly when equities fall —
they have low correlation.
So a slice of gold cushions your portfolio in a crash.
How much?
Around five to ten percent of your portfolio, as ballast —
a stabiliser, not the main engine of growth.
For traders, commodities offer trend-following, hedging,
and spread strategies like the gold-silver ratio.
But for the everyday investor,
gold's real job is quiet insurance.
Chapter nine, in brief.
Commodities — bullion, energy, and base metals —
trade on the MCX, mostly through leveraged futures.
Their prices are driven by global macro forces: the dollar,
interest rates, OPEC, and geopolitics.
But you don't need the leverage —
a gold ETF or a Sovereign Gold Bond lets you own gold calmly.
And gold's real value to a portfolio is as a hedge —
keep around five to ten percent as insurance, not as a bet.
Finally, the thread that ties everything together —
risk management.
